summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

key_cases.case_name: K.D. v. County of Crow Wing
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that emergency removal of a child without a court order is constitutionally permitted when continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child's health or welfare, and affirmed summary judgment for the Minnesota county and officers.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling constitutional standard for a Minnesota agency's decision to remove before obtaining a court order.
key_cases.quote: In cases in which continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child's health or welfare, emergency removal of children without a court order is constitutionally permitted.

key_cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed injunctive and declaratory relief, holding that the wholesale removal of boarding students on stale ex parte orders or with no order at all, absent exigent circumstances, violated the Fourth Amendment.
key_cases.relevance: It is the circuit's clearest example of an emergency-removal decision that failed constitutional scrutiny.
key_cases.quote: Waddle effected the wholesale removal of HCA's boarding students with ex parte orders or no orders at all in the absence of exigent circumstances

key_cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a Minnesota father's § 1983 claims, holding that a CHIPS petition filed two days after removal followed by a hearing within ten days supplied all the procedural process he was due.
key_cases.relevance: It is the most recent Eighth Circuit decision reviewing a Minnesota county's emergency removal and the process owed afterward.
key_cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that a Minnesota county social worker's 72-hour protective hold of a student under an ex parte order was objectively reasonable and that the order was not so lacking in probable cause as to make reliance on it unreasonable, granting qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: It shows when a caseworker may rely in good faith on an ex parte order to take a child into custody.
key_cases.quote: The ex parte order was not so lacking in indicia of probable cause as to render Diercks's reliance on it unreasonable.

timeline_requirements.deadline: Safety assessment completed at the face-to-face contact with the child and the child's primary caregiver, which must be sufficient to ensure the immediate safety of the child
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of a screened in report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Minn. Stat. § 260E.20; subd. 2(a) requires the face-to-face contact to be sufficient to complete a safety assessment and ensure the immediate safety of the child.

Not specified by statute; Minn. Stat. § 260E.24, subd. 3 requires the two determinations at the conclusion of the investigation and subd. 5 requires written notice within ten working days of that conclusion.

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Minn. Stat. § 260E.33; subd. 2 requires the written request within 15 calendar days after receipt of notice of the final determination, subd. 3 allows a fair hearing only after the agency denies the reconsideration request or fails to act on it within 15 working days, and subd. 1 provides no reconsideration after a family assessment or noncaregiver human trafficking assessment because no maltreatment determination is made.
